identity.name: Kairos
identity.gloss: Your answers put power and timing first: a strategic opening is an opportunity to act.

value.text: This reading notices shifts in leverage and the moments when available choices may narrow.
Keep options open until a consequential opening becomes clear.
Concentrate limited resources where they can change the immediate balance.
Act before a usable advantage closes or becomes more costly.
This reading accepts less consultation and continuity in exchange for timely, concentrated action.
This reading is strongest when delay would materially reduce the choices available.
Its strongest objection is that temporary leverage can displace legitimacy and longer-term consequences.
Its common failure mode is to mistake urgency for opportunity and press beyond a defensible aim.
The fit would weaken if durable rules reliably preserved options despite delay.
The fit would also weaken if using an advantage predictably created greater resistance than gain.
Order-first Kairos would use a strategic opening to preserve coexistence and prevent wider disorder.
Conditional Kairos would act only when the authority, stakes, and likely consequences justify the opening.
Justice-first Kairos would use leverage to protect obligations that settled arrangements leave unmet.
The Athenian argument at Melos treats unequal power as the decisive fact and presses an advantage before circumstances change.

whyItFits.qualification: This historical comparison uses provisional source metadata and remains pending research review.

value.text: The dialogue can also be read as Thucydides' indictment of imperial arrogance and overreach. It is an extreme episode, not a neutral summary of every realist position.

identity.name: Shi (勢)
identity.gloss: Power matters here as a position built over time; the priority is to establish leverage before forcing an outcome.

value.text: This reading notices the configuration of incentives, dependencies, and positions before open confrontation begins.
Build leverage before demanding a final decision.
Change incentives, alignments, or practical conditions before escalating.
Delay confrontation when time can improve the underlying position.
This reading accepts slower and less visible progress in exchange for a stronger position.
This reading is strongest when outcomes are shaped before the formal moment of choice.
Its strongest objection is that preparation can become indefinite delay or concealed manipulation.
Its common failure mode is to treat indirect leverage as control and underestimate adaptation by others.
The fit would weaken if urgent harm made delay more costly than positional improvement.
The fit would also weaken if other actors could readily neutralize the conditions being assembled.
Order-first Shi would shape conditions that preserve coexistence and reduce pressure for imposed settlements.
Conditional Shi would build position only where the authority, stakes, and likely consequences warrant it.
Justice-first Shi would reshape conditions so protection does not depend on accepting the existing hierarchy.
The Art of War repeatedly favors position, information, and strategic advantage over costly direct confrontation.

whyItFits.qualification: This historical comparison uses provisional source metadata and remains pending research review.

value.text: A military treatise is not a complete theory of international politics, and shi carries meanings that no two-sentence archetype can exhaust.

whereItBreaks.qualification: This historical comparison uses provisional source metadata and remains pending research review.

value.text: Shi is not only a classical term. 勢 and 大势 are in live use in contemporary PRC official discourse, where 大势 usually carries the sense of the trend of history moving in a settled direction. This archetype uses the strategic sense — build your own position rather than force the outcome — and does not import the contemporary political claim. Readers should know the word is doing current work as well as classical work.

identity.name: Grotian
identity.gloss: Your answers give rules force only when they are backed by credible enforcement.

analogue.label: Hugo Grotius / De Jure Belli ac Pacis

value.text: This reading notices where commitments lack clear rules, capable institutions, or credible consequences.
Translate shared commitments into specific duties and procedures.
Coordinate enough capacity to make agreed consequences credible.
Apply rules through procedures that remain legible and contestable.
This reading accepts less discretion and some coercive risk in exchange for dependable follow-through.
This reading is strongest when commitments repeatedly fail without a credible means of enforcement.
Its strongest objection is that enforcement power can be selective, unequal, and corrosive of legitimacy.
Its common failure mode is to equate compliance with legitimacy and extend enforcement beyond its mandate.
The fit would weaken if reciprocal compliance remained durable without coercive backing.
The fit would also weaken if enforcement produced evasion and fragmentation more reliably than compliance.
Order-first Grotian would enforce common rules to protect coexistence and restrain destabilizing breaches.
Conditional Grotian would calibrate enforcement to the authority, stakes, and likely consequences of the case.
Justice-first Grotian would enforce obligations even when powerful actors benefit from leaving them weak.

historicalAnalogue.label: Hugo Grotius / De Jure Belli ac Pacis

value.text: Grotius argued that relations among political communities remain subject to law and obligation, including during war.

whyItFits.qualification: This historical comparison uses provisional source metadata and remains pending research review.

value.text: The Grotian tradition is broader than enforcement. It also concerns natural law, consent, moral restraint, and the possibility of an international society.

whereItBreaks.qualification: This historical comparison uses provisional source metadata and remains pending research review.

value.text: This product already borrows from Martin Wight's three traditions elsewhere: Pluralist and Solidarist are English School terms. In that scheme, Grotian names the rationalist middle way between realism and revolutionism, not the enforcement-forward pole it marks here. The two senses collide. Readers who know Wight's usage should treat this name as a reference to Grotius's own argument that law binds even in war, not as a claim to the middle position in Wight's triad.

identity.name: Concert
identity.gloss: Durable cooperation here depends on powerful actors accepting rules and restraint.

value.text: This reading notices the interests, fears, and vetoes of actors able to disrupt a settlement.
Negotiate reciprocal limits before rivalry becomes harder to contain.
Create regular channels for consultation among consequential actors.
Accept bounded settlements when maximal demands would threaten the wider order.
This reading accepts incomplete inclusion and ambition in exchange for restraint among disruptive powers.
This reading is strongest when no durable order can survive without consent from its most capable challengers.
Its strongest objection is that accommodation can privilege powerful actors and marginalize weaker ones.
Its common failure mode is to confuse agreement among elites with a legitimate and durable settlement.
The fit would weaken if excluded actors could readily overturn the negotiated restraint.
The fit would also weaken if general rules constrained major powers more reliably than discretionary bargains.
Order-first Concert would use reciprocal restraint to preserve coexistence and prevent systemic breakdown.
Conditional Concert would bargain only where the authority, stakes, and likely consequences justify accommodation.
Justice-first Concert would seek consultation without granting powerful actors a veto over basic protection.
The Vienna settlement and the Concert joined great-power consultation to mutual restraint in the management of European order.

whyItFits.qualification: This historical comparison uses provisional source metadata and remains pending research review.

value.text: The Concert was hierarchical and exclusive. Its stability rested partly on spheres of influence and the limited voice of weaker states.

identity.name: Satyagraha
identity.gloss: Your answers treat shared beliefs as politically decisive: changing the public narrative can change what power achieves.

value.text: This reading notices the public meanings and legitimacy judgments that make authority easier or harder to sustain.
Reframe a dispute around the principle that gives it wider meaning.
Make contestation visible enough for an alternative standard to become imaginable.
Build a coalition around a different account of what conduct is acceptable.
This reading accepts slower material bargaining in exchange for clearer public contestation of legitimacy.
This reading is strongest when authority depends materially on public acceptance of its claims.
Its strongest objection is that persuasion can be overstated while coercion, organization, and material interests are understated.
Its common failure mode is to mistake symbolic visibility for durable change or shared moral agreement.
The fit would weaken if public reframing left the relevant incentives and institutions unchanged.
The fit would also weaken if the proposed standard lacked an organized path to implementation.
Order-first Satyagraha would contest legitimacy in ways intended to restore workable coexistence.
Conditional Satyagraha would calibrate contestation to the authority, stakes, and likely consequences involved.
Justice-first Satyagraha would challenge accepted standards when they leave protection or obligation unmet.

The Salt March broke a law in order to argue in public about its legitimacy, turning an ordinary commodity into a test of whether the colonial state could justify itself. Finnemore and Sikkink's norm life-cycle supplies the scholarly frame: a challenger contests an accepted standard, persuades an audience, and pushes a rival expectation toward acceptance.

whyItFits.qualification: This historical comparison uses provisional source metadata and remains pending research review.

value.text: The archetype cites a method, not a biography. Gandhi's own record is contested — most directly by B. R. Ambedkar on caste and varna, and separately over his writing and conduct on race during the South African years — and naming satyagraha is not an endorsement of the man or of his politics. Norm change is also not only narrative change: later research shows that localization, contestation, and implementation do not always follow a single linear cycle.

identity.name: Musyawarah
identity.gloss: Legitimacy here grows through patient consensus and cannot be secured by demand alone.

value.text: This reading notices relationships, procedural legitimacy, and objections that formal agreement may leave unspoken.
Consult before positions harden into public commitments.
Seek terms that differently situated participants can continue to live with.
Preserve room for dissent and further dialogue inside a collective decision.
This reading accepts slower and less ambitious decisions in exchange for broader ownership of the process.
This reading is strongest when implementation depends on trust and continuing consent among participants.
Its strongest objection is that consensus can conceal unequal pressure, dilute urgent duties, or reward obstruction.
Its common failure mode is to treat silence as consent and continue consultation after delay becomes decisive.
The fit would weaken if delay compounded harm that required a timely decision.
The fit would also weaken if nominal agreement concealed coercion or unresolved noncompliance.
Order-first Musyawarah would use deliberation to preserve coexistence, continuity, and mutual restraint.
Conditional Musyawarah would vary the needed consensus with the authority, stakes, and likely consequences.
Justice-first Musyawarah would deliberate broadly without allowing consensus to erase duties to excluded people.
ASEAN practice emphasizes consultation, consensus, informality, and avoiding public confrontation before collective decisions are announced.

whyItFits.qualification: This historical comparison uses provisional source metadata and remains pending research review.

value.text: Musyawarah and mufakat come from Malay and Indonesian practice and were generalized outward into a regional method; they do not describe every member state's tradition equally, and the ASEAN Way is internally contested. Consensus and non-interference can also prevent timely collective action.

identity.name: Dirigisme
identity.gloss: Your answers give production and finance a leading role, with the state actively shaping the dependencies they create.

value.text: This reading notices bottlenecks, investment gaps, and shared capacities that fragmented decisions may leave unresolved.
Direct finance toward capabilities judged strategically necessary.
Coordinate infrastructure and production where separate choices would work at cross-purposes.
Attach clear public conditions to support intended to shape investment.
This reading accepts less decentralization and greater capture risk in exchange for coordinated capacity.
This reading is strongest when fragmented incentives cannot produce a necessary shared capability in time.
Its strongest objection is that concentrated direction can entrench errors, favored interests, and weak correction.
Its common failure mode is to turn selective coordination into permanent protection or detailed control.
The fit would weaken if decentralized investment reliably supplied the necessary capacity on acceptable terms.
The fit would also weaken if public direction repeatedly misallocated resources and resisted correction.
Order-first Dirigisme would coordinate capacity to preserve continuity and meet basic collective needs.
Conditional Dirigisme would intervene where the authority, evidence, and constraints justify coordinated direction.
Justice-first Dirigisme would direct capacity toward unmet needs and unequally distributed burdens.

The Monnet Plan is dirigisme in its own language: a French planning commissariat concentrated postwar investment in a short list of basic sectors — coal, steel, electricity, rail transport, cement, farm machinery — and set targets that private firms were expected to meet.

whyItFits.qualification: This historical comparison uses provisional source metadata and remains pending research review.

value.text: Indicative planning steered investment; it did not replace markets or private ownership. The plan also depended on postwar reconstruction conditions, external aid, and a particular domestic coalition, so it is a weak guide to what state direction can do under different fiscal and political constraints.

identity.name: Dependencia
identity.gloss: Reducing external dependence is central to resilience in this result.

value.text: This reading notices external chokepoints, financing constraints, and dependencies that can narrow practical autonomy.
Diversify suppliers, finance, and markets where concentration creates asymmetric exposure.
Build domestic or regional capacity where exit is otherwise prohibitively costly.
Preserve policy space by reducing dependence on any single external gatekeeper.
This reading accepts some efficiency and access costs in exchange for greater room to choose.
This reading is strongest when concentrated external dependence makes formal choice difficult to exercise.
Its strongest objection is that dependence can be reciprocal and diversification can create costly new constraints.
Its common failure mode is to treat all interdependence as domination and create new vulnerabilities through insulation.
The fit would weaken if open ties dispersed leverage and made switching inexpensive.
The fit would also weaken if domestic constraints explained the loss of autonomy better than external structure.
Order-first Dependencia would reduce dependencies that threaten continuity, coexistence, and practical autonomy.
Conditional Dependencia would target dependencies whose asymmetry, stakes, and likely consequences justify the cost.
Justice-first Dependencia would restructure dependencies that reproduce unequal burdens or deny meaningful agency.
Prebisch's centre-periphery analysis treated trade and production structures as durable constraints on development and national room for action.

whyItFits.qualification: This historical comparison uses provisional source metadata and remains pending research review.

value.text: Prebisch's reformist structuralism preceded and differed from several later dependencia schools. Reducing exposure is only one possible response to dependency.
